title: India's Diaspora Deposits Record $127 Billion Under RBI Scheme, Exceeding All Estimates
excerpt: The RBI's special FCNR window drew five times the inflows of its 2013 predecessor, pushing forex reserves to a record $729 billion and lifting the rupee to a two-month high.
body:
• India mobilized $127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits from its overseas diaspora, exceeding the RBI's $80 billion target by over 70%
  • Total foreign currency inflows hit $136.38 billion, pushing reserves to a record $729.33 billion and giving the central bank fresh ammunition to defend the rupee
  • The RBI closed the deposit window a month early on August 31, after banks including SBI, ICICI, HSBC, and Standard Chartered mounted an aggressive global campaign offering rates up to 7.75%
  • Economists warn the massive inflow creates liquidity-management challenges and a future dollar-denominated repayment obligation worth roughly 1 trillion rupees in lower RBI dividends

India drew a record $127.23 billion from its 35-million-strong overseas diaspora through a special foreign-currency deposit program, far surpassing the Reserve Bank of India's original $80 billion estimate and handing policymakers their most formidable buffer to defend the rupee in over a decade.

The deposits were raised through the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR(B), scheme launched in June after the rupee hit record lows earlier this year. Including external commercial borrowings of $3.89 billion and overseas foreign-currency borrowings of $5.26 billion, total inflows reached $136.38 billion by August 31, according to the RBI.

A 'Stratospheric' Response

The scale of the response stunned markets. Nomura analysts Sonal Varma and Aurodeep Nandi described the result as "stratospheric," noting the inflows give the RBI ample "fire power" to manage currency volatility amid rising oil prices and global bond sell-offs.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=zOIrgZiHr5o

"This is clearly larger than expectations. This should give comfort to the RBI on currency, and their ability to manage volatility."

— Vivek Rajpal, Asia strategist at JB Drax Honore

The scheme revives a playbook India used during the 2013 taper tantrum, when a similar FCNR window attracted roughly $26 billion and fueled a sharp rupee rally. This time, the response was nearly five times larger, reflecting both the growth of India's diaspora wealth and the aggressive push by lenders to capture deposits.

How Banks Mounted a Global Campaign

An aggressive, coordinated drive by Indian and international banks turned what is typically a steady stream of diaspora deposits into a torrent. State Bank of India, ICICI Bank, HSBC Holdings, and Standard Chartered reached out to non-resident Indians through branches, relationship managers, and diaspora networks across Dubai, Singapore, London, and other major hubs.

The RBI sweetened the deal by absorbing the currency-hedging costs of FCNR deposits. Banks, in turn, passed on interest rates as high as 7.75% to overseas Indians, making the deposits significantly more attractive than comparable options in Western markets. Lenders also used India's tax-free financial hub, Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), to channel approximately $52.82 billion under the RBI's swap window, according to Bloomberg.

The overwhelming response prompted the RBI to close the deposit window a full month ahead of its originally scheduled September 30 deadline, saying its objective had been achieved.

Rupee Rallies, Reserves Hit Record

Markets reacted immediately. The rupee strengthened as much as 0.7% to 94.2713 per dollar, its highest level in more than a month. The yield on the 10-year sovereign bond declined 4 basis points to 6.94%, and the Nifty Bank Index rose as much as 0.9% in early trading.

India's foreign exchange reserves climbed to a record $729.33 billion as of the week ending August 21, equivalent to roughly 11 months of import cover. Gaura Sen Gupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank, projected India's current account could reflect a surplus of as much as $80 billion for the year through March, a dramatic reversal from earlier deficit fears.

The Other Side of the Ledger

The record haul is not without complications. The conversion of foreign currency into rupees has pushed banking system liquidity to a record 9.7 trillion rupees ($102.66 billion), creating a sterilization challenge for the RBI.

At a meeting with the central bank, bank executives proposed using foreign exchange sell/buy swaps to gradually drain excess rupee liquidity, according to Reuters. A unanimous preference for forex swaps over increases to the cash reserve ratio reflected banks' concerns about margin compression.

"Given the magnitude of these inflows, its profitable deployment is likely to take some time and could intensify competition for quality borrowers."

— Sachin Sachdeva, Vice President, ICRA

Madhavi Arora, lead economist at Emkay Global Financial Services, noted the deposits represent a future dollar-denominated debt liability maturing in three and five years. She estimated the indirect fiscal cost, through potentially lower RBI dividends, at roughly 1 trillion rupees cumulatively.

What This Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, the scheme underscored both the community's growing financial clout and the tangible returns available to those who participate. Interest rates of up to 7.75% on dollar-denominated deposits, with the RBI bearing hedging costs, offered a risk-adjusted return well above most Western savings instruments.

The FCNR(B) deposit window is now closed, but the window for bank borrowings remains open. The success of the program is likely to inform future RBI interventions and reinforce the diaspora's role as a financial backstop during periods of external stress.
